AFDRAH

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
806 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* Minor PoP adjustments for this weekend, otherwise no major changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 245 PM Friday...

1) Unsettled wx pattern this weekend, potentially wet at times later 
Saturday. 

2) Mainly dry with temps closer to seasonable values much of next 
week. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 245 PM Friday...

1) Unsettled wx pattern this weekend, potentially wet at times later 
Saturday. 

An upper short wave trough currently moving across the Miss Valley 
will lift NE across the TN Valley tomorrow and exit off the Mid-
Atlantic coast by mid-day Sunday.  In response, we'll see several 
opportunities for showers and tstms through early Sunday, the first 
of which being widely scattered showers and tstms the rest of today, 
a few of which could include an isolated strong or possibly damaging 
wind gust (see SWODY1 for additional details).  

Saturday, particularly later in the day and early night, appears to 
be the most unsettled part of the weekend as the trough approaches 
and begins moving across. While a shower/tstm will be possible any 
time Saturday, the most likely time and best coverage will likely be 
late in the day from mid-afternoon hours through the late evening 
hours. It's worth noting that central NC is included in the Days 1 
and 2 ERO, so any of the heavier downpours could results in isold 
flooding of the typical spots that are more sensitive to heavy 
downpours, such as urban and low-lying areas. 

While the bulk of the prefrontal shower/tstm activity should be to 
our east by daybreak Sunday morning, we can't rule out a few 
additional showers or tstms assoc with the actual frontal passage 
which will occur later Sunday, thus the reason for the ongoing 
elevated PoPs Sunday afternoon; however, coverage and intensity 
should be much less compared to the previous day.  

2) Mainly dry with temps closer to seasonable values much of next 
week.  

Most of next week will be dry thanks to an upper ridge that will be 
positioned to our west much of the time and resulting dry northerly 
flow. In addition, the airmass... while still a few deg above 
normal... will at least be closer to normal with highs each day 
generally in the 80s.  It's worth noting that a closed upper trough, 
broken off from a larger-scale trough moving off the Northeast 
states early next week, will drift south parallel to the East Coast. 
 Today's NWP models forecast it to remain far enough offshore so 
that our only impact from it will be occasional gusty NE winds at 
times during the mid-week period. 

&&

.AVIATION /00Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/... 
As of 800 PM Friday...

VFR will largely prevail across central NC through this evening, 
with mostly mid and high clouds. Isolated showers and storms have 
developed across mainly far northern and far southern parts of the 
region, along with a developing cluster near RDU. Brief heavy rain, 
lightning, and gusty winds will be possible with any storm, but 
other than what is currently happening around RDU, the chances of a 
storm directly impacting a terminal are low. 

Overnight tonight after about 06z, low stratus will begin to spread 
into central NC from north to south, with all terminals likely to 
experience IFR conditions. A period of LIFR is even possible around 
daybreak, along with patchy MVFR/IFR visibilities. VFR will return to 
most areas by midday on Saturday, but MVFR may linger into early 
afternoon around the Triad. Showers and storms are then expected to 
develop in the afternoon across the region, and they should be more 
widespread compared to today. Brief gusty winds and sub-VFR 
conditions will be possible with any storms.

Outlook: Shower and thunderstorm chances will continue through 
Saturday evening as a cold front makes its way through central NC.
Low stratus and/or fog may develop and cause sub-VFR restrictions 
again on Sunday and Monday mornings as well. 

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

FXUS62 KILM 120002
AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
800 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Aviation section updated. 

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

2) Well-above normal temperatures and high humidity will 
maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 degrees through 
Monday.

3) A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

This morning's 12z CHS weather balloon measured a precipitable 
water of 2.35 inches. That's one-third of an inch above the 90th
climatological percentile and near the daily max for this time 
of year. Deep Gulf moisture will continue to stream northeastward
across the eastern Carolinas through Sunday morning between a 
mid level ridge east of the Bahamas and a trough over the Mid-
Mississippi Valley.

Surface-based CAPE near 2000 J/kg, forecast 0-6 km bulk shear
around 10 knots, and little-to-no dry air aloft argues for
single-cell storm development on Saturday with heavy rain 
potential. Some loose storm organization could occur along the 
seabreeze front and any outflow boundaries, but severe weather 
risk should remain very low. HREF ensemble 24-hr max precip of 
3-5 inches implies there will be a few isolated heavy totals 
within the sea of 0.25 to 0.50 inch weekend amounts.

The upper trough producing the break in the ridge should slide 
eastward across the Carolinas on Sunday, perhaps enhancing bulk
shear to around 20 knots. Multicells should become possible, 
perhaps bringing better potential for gusty winds. The upper 
trough should shift offshore Sunday night ahead of rising mid 
and upper level heights spreading eastward from the Mid South.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Well-above normal temperatures and high humidity will 
maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 degrees through 
Monday.

850 mb temps in the +18C to +19C range should continue through
the weekend. This is at or above the 90th climatological 
percentile for mid September. If it weren't for the increased 
cloudiness and convection expected this weekend we'd probably be
looking at Heat Advisory-level conditions. 

As it stands now, forecast highs in the upper 80s to around 90 
coupled with dewpoints well into the 70s should yield heat 
indices in the 100-103 range through Monday.

NWS ILM has never issued a Heat Advisory later than September 5
since the introduction of VTEC product codes twenty years ago.
(and that latest advisory was earlier this month)


KEY MESSAGE 3...A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

Models have all come into line over the past 24 hours showing
the strongest Canadian high we've seen since last Spring moving
across New England Tuesday into Wednesday. This should push a
cold front southward across the eastern Carolinas Monday night,
allowing a modified Canadian airmass to spread across the area
Tuesday into Wednesday. This won't be crisp, dry Canadian air by
any means given its long passage across water temps in the 70s 
and 80s, but it should bring cooler air across the area knocking
temperatures back down closer to normal for mid September.

Forecast lows in particular look refreshing with 60s expected
for all but east-facing beaches Tuesday night and Wednesday
night. Some inland locations could conceivably dip to 60
degrees.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...

VFR for most of tonight until we head towards the predawn hours.
Late tonight there is a moderate potential for LIFR ceilings to
develop over KFLO and KLBT mainly after 10z, lingering through 13-
14z much like we saw this morning. Guidance has backed off slightly 
on both but given not only the ambient moisture in place but the 
widespread rainfall we saw these solutions have not been favored and 
the forecast remains rather pessimistic. The low clouds should limit 
fog vsby restrictions to MVFR. These low stratus clouds should lift 
into a cumulus cloud deck with bases 2500-3500 feet AGL after 14-15z 
Saturday with another round of showers and thunderstorms anticipated 
to develop during the heat of the day.

Extended Outlook...Scattered showers and thunderstorms bringing
brief MVFR/IFR conditions are expected Saturday afternoon and
again Sunday afternoon. There is also a low potential for late 
night/early morning stratus or ground fog affecting KLBT and 
KFLO late Saturday night and again late Sunday night. VFR
conditions should prevail Monday through Wednesday as a more
stable and drier Canadian airmass builds in from the northeast.

&&

.MARINE...
Tonight through Tuesday night...Models continue to consistently
show a cold front stalling across interior North Carolina 
tonight, then lifting back north on Saturday with no direct 
impact on our weather or winds this far south. Light to moderate
southwesterly winds are expected to continue through the 
weekend along with multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms 
Saturday through Sunday night. 

Drier weather should develop on Monday as high pressure
strengthens aloft over the Carolinas. The strongest Canadian
high we've seen since last Spring should move across New England
Tuesday and Wednesday, pushing a cold front southward across the
Carolina coastal waters Monday night. Northeast winds behind the
front should increase to a solid 20 knots offshore and 15-20 
knots nearshore Tuesday into Tuesday night. Seas within 20 
miles of shore could build to 4-6 feet with dominant wave
periods near 6 seconds.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 9 PM this evening to 1 AM EDT 
     Saturday for NCZ107.
SC...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

MARINE...TRA

AFDJAX

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
729 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Moderate Rip Current Risk all Local Beaches Today and Friday.
Elevated Risk Returns Early Next Week

- Daily Heat Index up to 107 through Sunday

- Daily Afternoon & Evening Thunderstorms. Main Hazards: Locally
Heavy Rain, Lightning & Gusty Winds Up to 40-50 mph

&&

.NEAR TERM /UNTIL 6 AM SATURDAY MORNING/...
Main Highlights:

- Numerous Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Expected through 
Saturday. Strong Storm Potential Along the I-95 Corridor   During 
the Late Afternoon Hours. Stronger Storms May Produce   Wind Gusts 
of 40-55 mph, Frequent Lightning Strikes, and   Torrential Downpours 
that Could Result in Localized Flooding.

- Daily Peak Heat Index Values of 104-108 Degrees Expected. through 
Monday.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk Continues at All Area Beaches through 
Monday. High Risk Likely from Tuesday through Thursday. 

Afternoon surface analysis depicts weakening Atlantic high pressure 
(1019 millibars) situated off the southeastern seaboard, with this 
feature extending its axis westward across north central FL. 
Meanwhile, a frontal boundary stretching from North Carolina's Outer 
Banks westward across the Tennessee Valley and the Ozarks was in the 
process of stalling as another weak high pressure center stretches 
across the Great Lakes, Mid-Atlantic states and New England in the 
wake of this boundary. Aloft...deep-layered ridging was centered 
just northeast of the Bahamas, which was directing a shortwave 
trough  located on the western periphery of this feature north-
northeastward across western portions of the FL panhandle. 
Otherwise, a potent shortwave trough was digging eastward across the 
Ozarks towards the Tennessee Valley. Latest GOES-East derived Total 
Precipitable Water imagery indicates that deep tropical moisture 
remains in place area-wide, with PWAT values generally in the 2 - 
2.3 inch range across our area. Convection on the leading edge of 
the shortwave trough that was crossing western portions of the FL 
panhandle has crossed the Alapaha and Suwannee Rivers, with only 
isolated showers located elsewhere, mainly at inland locations. 
Temperatures at 18Z were generally in the upper 80s and lower 90s, 
with dewpoints mostly in the low to mid 70s creating heat index 
values mostly around 100. 

Abundant tropical moisture and continued slow cooling of 
temperatures aloft should allow for showers and thunderstorms to 
become numerous across our region as the afternoon progresses, with 
southwesterly steering flow bringing convection towards the I-95 
corridor late this afternoon, where activity could linger into the 
early evening hours. The presence of a pinned Atlantic sea breeze 
boundary along the I-95 corridor and other mesoscale boundary 
collisions should allow for storms to "pulse" and potentially become 
strong later this afternoon, especially as convection intersects the 
Atlantic sea breeze boundary that should be positioned near I-95. 
Storms that pulse and become strong will be capable of producing 
downburst winds of 40-50 mph, along with frequent lightning strikes 
and torrential downpours. Given the deep tropical moisture in place, 
any storms that "back-build" along mesoscale boundaries such as the 
Atlantic sea breeze could result in localized flooding, especially 
if this potential event occurs at urban or low-lying, normally flood 
prone locations. 

Convection could linger into the early to mid evening hours tonight, 
especially along the I-95 corridor in southeast GA, where convection 
may not arrive until later this afternoon. Otherwise, debris cloud 
cover will thin out after midnight, with deepening southwesterly 
flow likely developing a greater coverage of predawn convection over 
Apalachee Bay than what was observed this morning. Some of this 
activity could move onshore along the FL Big Bend and Nature Coasts 
towards sunrise, but activity should remain west of the Suwannee 
River and north central FL through the early morning hours on 
Saturday. Lows will fall to the low and mid 70s across most of our 
area.

&&

.SHORT TERM /6 AM SATURDAY MORNING THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Main Highlights This Period:

- Potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and localized flooding 
on Saturday

Southwest steering flow continues to bring in enhanced moisture 
(PWATs 2.2-2.4") across the area, prompting numerous showers and 
storms Saturday afternoon and evening. The Gulf sea breeze will push 
further inland, meeting the Atlantic sea breeze closer to the east 
coast/I-95 corridor, which is where our best chance for strong 
thunderstorm development will be. Gusty winds will be the primary 
threat with any strong storms, but also heavy rainfall may cause 
localized flooding concerns, especially in urban and typically flood 
prone areas. High temperatures Saturday will be in the low 90s, with 
max afternoon heat index values peaking around 104-107 for portions 
of northeast Florida.

Convection is expected to be less widespread on Sunday as the high 
pressure ridge shifts northward and crosses over the forecast area, 
with the prevailing flow gradually shifting to a more northeasterly 
onshore flow by the beginning of next week. Overall, precipitation 
chances will be about 20-40% across much of the area, with higher 
chances over north central Florida. Similar high temperatures are 
expected Sunday, in the lower 90s.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Main Highlights This Period Monday through Thursday: 

- Daily Thunderstorms Potential Each Day Next Week

- Elevated Rip Current Risk Next Week 

Northwesterly flow Monday gradually shifts to northeasterly Tuesday, 
beginning a few day period of stronger onshore flow through 
Thursday. Tuesday through Thursday, those breezy easterly surface 
winds will bring showers and isolated thunderstorms onshore in the 
mornings, with coverage expanding inland throughout the day. For 
daily afternoon and evening storms, the focus will be generally 
south of I-10 each day. High temperatures gradually lower throughout 
the week, Monday highs will be in the lower to mid 90s, and by 
Thursday areas closer to the east coast will peak in the mid 80s.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z SATURDAY THROUGH 00Z SUNDAY/...
Convection/TSRA activity ending early this evening as line of storms 
pushes into the Atlantic waters with just lingering IFR conds at SSI 
until 01Z. Otherwise mostly VFR conds this evening with mid/high 
clouds slowly dissipating, then the usual chances of LIFR CIGS and 
IFR VSBYS in low stratus/fog at VQQ/GNV from 08-12Z, with much lower 
chances at the coastal TAF sites towards sunrise. Light SW flow and 
diurnal heating will trigger afternoon showers and storms at all TAF 
sites Saturday afternoon and for now have added PROB30 groups at all 
terminals from 17-23Z for TSRA activity with gusty winds and MVFR 
conds for now, with timing to be refined in later TAF forecasts.

&&

.MARINE...


Weakening high pressure situated off the southeastern seaboard will 
continue to shift southward as a frontal boundary stalls across the 
Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas. The axis of this feature will 
remain south of our local waters through the weekend, resulting in 
prevailing south to southwest winds, with the afternoon sea breeze 
providing onshore winds for the near shore waters. Thunderstorms 
will likely develop over coastal locations during the mid to late 
afternoon hours that will generally progress eastward across our 
local waters during the late afternoon and evening hours through the 
weekend, with a few stronger storms containing strong wind gusts, 
frequent lightning strikes, and torrential downpours possible each 
afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, high pressure strengthening over 
the Great Lakes region in the wake of a cold front on Sunday and 
Monday will wedge down the southeastern seaboard by Tuesday and 
Wednesday. Onshore winds will develop across our local waters on 
Monday night, followed by northeasterly winds strengthening on 
Tuesday and especially Tuesday night and Wednesday, when a period of 
Small Craft Advisory conditions will be possible, accompanied by 
building seas that will likely persist through Thursday.

Rip Currents: Offshore winds during the morning hours through 
Monday will tend to reduce the rip current risk at area beaches. The 
afternoon sea breeze will create breakers of 2-3 feet at the 
northeast FL beaches, which will combine with a lingering easterly 
ocean swell to create a lower end moderate risk, especially during 
the outgoing tide. Breakers of only 1-2 feet at the southeast GA 
beaches will likely yield a low risk through Monday. Northeasterly 
winds will develop on Monday night and will likely become breezy on 
Tuesday, likely resulting in a high risk at all area beaches from 
the afternoon hours through at least Thursday as breakers build.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

Diurnal southwesterly winds will persist through the end of the week 
and through the weekend. As a result of the moist southwesterly 
flow, the diurnal east coast sea breeze will be pinned near the 
shoreline and not reach inland much past the I-95 corridor. Flow 
pattern is expected to shift to become more onshore by the beginning 
of next week.

Fog Potential: Gusty and erratic wind shifts will occur from 
thunderstorm activity. Patchy fog is expected across inland areas 
the next couple of mornings, with widespread dense fog unlikely.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...
As far as coastal water levels, coastal water levels will remain 
near and below action stage despite the new moon phase today.

As far as rainfall again today, isolated pockets of up to 3-4 inches 
are possible mainly the St Johns River Basin northward to near or 
just south of Waycross and Nahunta. These storms may cause temporary 
flooding, especially in any poor drainage or urbanized areas.

&&

.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  72  92  73  92 /  40  50  30  20 
SSI  77  88  76  91 /  50  50  30  30 
JAX  74  91  74  92 /  40  60  30  40 
SGJ  74  90  74  91 /  40  60  30  40 
GNV  73  92  73  91 /  30  60  30  40 
OCF  73  92  73  92 /  30  60  30  70 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
605 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Very warm today with only isolated high based showers/virga 
  late this afternoon and evening.

- Slight increase in shower/storm coverage this weekend. Cooler
  Saturday, then warmer Sunday.

- Unsettled pattern next week, with multiple cold fronts expected
  to bring a few more noticeable cooldowns.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Friday/...
Issued at 1245 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

This morning's wave cloud kept some heat relief in place for the 
northern corridor for the first half of the day. Now that the 
cloud has dissipated, temperatures are quickly heating, with KLMO 
seeing an eight degree warming in the past hour alone.
Temperatures were adjusted slightly to account for the cooler 
morning, but we are still expecting a hot day across the lower 
elevations due to downsloping winds and a slight warming in 
temperatures aloft. Water vapor imagery shows moisture has
slightly increased in the westerly flow aloft through the morning.
We still expect some isolated high-based showers to develop this 
afternoon over the higher elevations, with some virga showers
expected to bring gusty outflows to the lower elevations. We may
manage to squeeze a few sprinkles out of some of them, but mostly
just expect 30-40 mph winds as virga passes over for areas east of
the mountains. 

A cold front is expected late tonight/early Saturday morning that
will bring some gusty northerly winds across the plains and 
cooler temperatures for Saturday. A slight increase in moisture 
is expected with the front as well. Afternoon showers and a few
storms will be possible, with the best chances being over the
northern mountains where instability will be greatest, but can't
rule out some holding together long enough to push off the higher
elevations. Have added a mention of at least slight chance for
PoPs to the forecast across the northern plains and areas along 
the Palmer Divide. 

Sunday is still on track to be the hottest day of the week in
between cold fronts. While the NBM seems to have a warm bias, most
guidance does show afternoon highs in the low to mid 90s, so
afternoon highs were trimmed back slightly to be more in line with
the majority of guidance. Either way, it will still be hot for the
second week of September. There will be some better instability 
in place across the northeast plains that if tapped into, could 
allow for some stronger to severe storms in the afternoon/evening. 

Not much has changed in the long term forecast today, with the
northern tier still expected to remain active over the next week.
A few cold fronts are still progged to bring a few more cooldowns
through the week, and afternoon showers and storms will be 
possible each afternoon. 

&&

.AVIATION /00Z TAFS through 00Z Sunday/...
Issued at 603 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

VFR expected through the TAF period. Current radar imagery shows a 
push of WNW winds moving through the Denver metro as well as a few 
microbursts in the vicinity of KDEN. Virga showers and gusty 
outflows will continue to be possible through 02Z this evening. 
Winds will become southerly later tonight before a cold front tracks 
through the terminals between 09Z and 11Z, bringing a N-NE wind 
shift. 

Another round of virga showers will be possible tomorrow afternoon, 
likely starting at ~22Z. Although conditions look slightly less 
favorable than today, a few microbursts with gusty winds up to 
30KT cannot be ruled out, particularly near KAPA and KBJC. We 
have kept a PROB30 out of the TAF for KDEN at this time given low 
confidence in convection being able to survive off of the 
foothills and Palmer Divide, but it may need to be added if 
future guidance suggests otherwise. 

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$
